verses.note: Paul reads this verse against the risen Christ: the first Adam received life, the last Adam gives it (1 Corinthians 15:45). The resurrection is pictured as a new act of the creator who first breathed life into dust, and Ezekiel's valley of bones uses the same image of breath entering bodies.

The hope that God could give Isaac back from death is not stated in Genesis but drawn from it by Hebrews 11:19, which calls Isaac's return a figure of resurrection. The verse contributes a trust in God's promise that reaches past the point where death seems to end it.

Jesus appeals to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, all eventually laid in this cave, to argue that God is the God of the living (Matthew 22:31-32). The grave at Machpelah becomes part of the Bible's case for resurrection.

Jesus quotes this verse to answer the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection. God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths, and Jesus draws the conclusion that he is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26-27). The covenant relationship God claims with the patriarchs, long dead when he speaks, implies that death has not ended it.

Peter argues that David died and his tomb was still in Jerusalem, so the words point beyond him to the Messiah whose body did not decay (Acts 2:29-31). The church's confession of the bodily resurrection gives the verse its fullest sense.

The psalm's turn from death's dust to praise, with the answer arriving at the last moment, became for the church the shape of Good Friday turning to Easter. Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered prayers with loud cries to the one able to save him from death and was heard.

After being cut off from the land of the living (verse 8) and buried (verse 9), the Servant sees offspring and prolongs his days. The song does not explain how, but it plainly speaks of life beyond his death. The New Testament reads this vindication as fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, according to the Scriptures).

In context the graves are the exile and the resurrection is the return. But the metaphor depends on the conviction that God can raise the dead, and it prepared the way for the explicit hope of Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.15.1) and Tertullian (On the Resurrection of the Flesh) cited this passage against those who denied the body's resurrection. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 92b) records rabbis debating whether the dead of Ezekiel's valley were actually raised, one sage calling the vision a parable and others insisting it happened.
